summary: This informational RFC describes the IETF architecture for a standard programmatic interface for state transfer in and out of the Internet routing system, covering the high-level architecture, its building blocks and interfaces, with focus on those to be standardized for I2RS.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan for how software can read from and write to routers in a standard way.

questions: interface to the routing system architecture
what is an i2rs agent and client
what is ephemeral state in i2rs
how does i2rs handle conflicting writes
subtitle: How software applications can read and write routing state through clients and agents on routers.

tldr.problem: Applications that want to learn network state or program forwarding-related state have no common, standard, fast interface to the routing system; each router offers different information, mechanisms and CLI.
tldr.mechanism: I2RS places an agent on each routing element and a client with each application, speaking an asynchronous, data-model-driven protocol that reads state, subscribes to events and writes ephemeral state, with identity, roles and priorities to keep it safe and predictable.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the architecture and the properties required of the protocol and models; the protocol itself reuses NETCONF and RESTCONF with YANG 1.1 data models.

today: RFC 7921 is an Informational document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the architecture, and it points to RFC 7920 for the problem statement and to separate documents for the detailed protocol and security requirements.

sections.title: The Problem I2RS Solves
sections.content:
Routers keep state at many layers. A typical router maintains a Routing Information Base (RIB), runs protocols such as OSPF, IS-IS and BGP, and turns the result into forwarding entries. Network-oriented applications want easy access to this information to learn topology, check that programmed state is installed in the forwarding plane, and measure flows, and they also want an interface to program forwarding-related state.

The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) is a programmatic, asynchronous interface for moving state into and out of the Internet routing system. The RFC gives four drivers: an interface that is programmatic and asynchronous with fast, interactive access for atomic operations; access to structured state that is often not modeled in existing configuration protocols; filterable event notifications; and operation driven by data models. The problem statement is in RFC 7920.

I2RS also allows injecting ephemeral state, which does not survive a reboot of the device or of the software handling I2RS. It only permits changes that could be made through Local Configuration; direct manipulation of protocol-internal, dynamically determined data is not envisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router speaks its own dialect. I2RS gives programs one common language to ask routers what is happening and to give them temporary instructions.

sections.title: Clients, Agents and Routing Elements
sections.content:
Applications reach I2RS services through I2RS clients. A client can serve one or more applications and can be local (on the same box as the routing system) or remote. Each client can talk to one or more I2RS agents, and each agent can serve many clients. The agent is part of a Routing Element, which implements some subset of the routing system and need not have a forwarding plane. Agent and client use an asynchronous protocol, so a client can post several requests at once and an agent can process requests from many clients simultaneously.

The agent gives read and write access to selected data, organized into I2RS services, and lets clients subscribe to notifications. Terms that scope access are the read scope, write scope and notification scope. Access is tied to an identity, which has roles, and a client may also pass a secondary opaque identifier so that actions can be attributed to the application behind it.

On the router side the agent works with routing and signaling, Local Configuration, dynamic system state (counters, statistics, local events) and static system state (such as queueing behavior). The scope of I2RS is the interaction between agent and client, not how applications talk to a remote client.
sections.plainLanguage: An app is like a customer, the client is its waiter, and the agent is the kitchen on the router. Many waiters can talk to many kitchens at the same time.

sections.title: Simplicity, Extensibility and Data Models
sections.content:
Three architectural properties are stressed. Simplicity: the amount of information and its variety could easily make the protocol complex, so for each component the authors ask whether the complexity is needed or merely nice to have. Overly complex data models tend to ossify information sets.

Extensibility: the work is phased, so the data models, and also the primitives and protocol operations, must be easy to extend. Model-driven interfaces: many routing components are standardized but their data models are not, so each router uses different information, mechanisms and CLI. With models, a client implements only the models it accesses, an agent only those it supports, and tools can automatically check and manipulate data. Each service can correspond to its own data model, and an agent may indicate which models it supports.

For variation between devices, the information models can use class inheritance with base and sub classes, clearly marked optional parts, and templates. They must also express relationships between objects, from simple initialization by copying to actively coupled state.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is keep it simple and leave room to grow. Like building blocks, a program only needs the pieces for the job it is doing.

sections.title: How the Agent Handles State and Conflicts
sections.content:
The agent keeps the I2RS datastore: the changes it applied, who asked for them, and active subscriptions. State stays until the client removes it, another operation such as the CLI overrides it, or the device reboots. After a reboot the agent does not reapply it. When state is removed, it reverts to what it would have been without I2RS, and the agent does not store multiple alternatives the way a RIB stores routes at different preferences.

If the agent fails, it MUST support two notifications: NOTIFICATION_I2RS_AGENT_TERMINATING for graceful shutdown (with an optional timestamp of no finer than one second granularity) and NOTIFICATION_I2RS_AGENT_STARTING, which carries an agent-boot-count so a client can tell the agent restarted.

Changes can come from Local Configuration or from I2RS. Operator policy decides which wins; most devices are expected to let ephemeral data override Local Configuration, but the general rule is that by default Local Configuration wins, so that I2RS can be installed and tested without it overwriting anything. Resolution is based on source priority, not time, because most-recent-wins could cause non-deterministic race conditions. If two clients try to write the same data, that is an error case, but the highest priority remains in effect and ties go to the first client attributed to the data. Writes through different clients to the same list, such as a prefix list, are not an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes written in pencil can be erased. I2RS instructions are pencil notes on the router, and if two people write on the same line, the more important person wins.

sections.title: The Client-Agent Interface
sections.content:
The architecture assumes a data-model-driven protocol with models in YANG 1.1, and names NETCONF and RESTCONF as the protocols to be expanded for I2RS. It allows several transports (TCP, SCTP, DCCP) with authentication, integrity protection and congestion control. Each protocol version must say which transports are mandatory and which are optional.

Several communication channels are expected, and the protocol may be carried in-band through the data plane or out-of-band through a management interface. Because a client need not keep a connection open, an agent may open a new channel to deliver requested information. Capability negotiation is kept simple: basic version negotiation, then capability models for each service.

Clients can register for filtered notifications of events, and information collection (snapshots and feeds of changes) is treated as architecturally separate because of its higher rate and volume. There are no multi-message transactions or rollback; instead one message with several operations can use one of three error-handling modes, and the protocol explicitly replies even to successful writes.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are sent by existing router talk, like using an existing phone line. A single message can say stop at the first mistake, do all or none, or try everything and report the failures.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says I2RS clearly requires serious security consideration. The assumed environment is that the agent is a trusted part of its Routing Element, with a separate authentication and authorization channel, and that mutual authentication between client and agent is required. A client is not automatically trustworthy; its identity and role limit what it can ask. Authorization uses the lower of the permissions of the agent and the authenticated client.

Control exchanges should be authenticated and integrity-protected, and manipulation must be accurately attributable. The primary channel used to authenticate and write needs integrity, confidentiality and replay protection, while other streams may need less. Because an agent may open a channel based on information supplied by a client, such requests must come from an authenticated and authorized client. The RFC also covers client redundancy, privacy issues when an agent or client is tied to a person such as on a phone, and the need for resource limits and traceability for operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Only verified visitors may touch the router's controls, and each gets only the keys that fit their job. Everything they do is written in a logbook.

viz.caption: THE THREE ERROR-HANDLING MODES FOR A MULTI-OPERATION MESSAGE

items.title: Perform all or none
items.text: The agent keeps enough state to roll back; either every operation succeeds or none is applied.

items.title: Perform until error
items.text: Operations are applied in order; on an error, no further operations are applied.

items.title: Perform all storing errors
items.text: The agent attempts every operation and returns an error for each one that fails.
